title: AI Feedback on Drafts
targetBand: Mục tiêu luyện tập theo tiêu chí mức 5/5 của rubric Discussion; không bảo đảm điểm Writing 5.5–6.0

prompt.professorQuestion: In our class, we are discussing AI feedback on drafts. One proposal is that teachers should allow AI feedback on early drafts; another is that teachers should limit such tools. Which approach would you support, and what limitation would you consider?

studentOpinions.stance: I would support the first approach: teachers should allow AI feedback on early drafts. It can flag unclear sentences before students seek human help. The immediate benefit matters because people need a workable solution in everyday life. We could review the results after a short period and improve the details if necessary.

I see a stronger case for the second approach: teachers should limit such tools. Students may accept suggestions without learning to revise. A policy can sound promising yet create costs or problems for people it overlooks. Starting with the less disruptive choice would give us time to understand those effects.

prompt.recommendedWords: Ít nhất 100 từ theo đề mẫu ETS; 120–150 từ là mục tiêu luyện tập

modelEssay: I agree more with Michael on AI feedback on drafts, although Sarah identifies an important limit. It can flag unclear sentences before students seek human help. The key is whether the tool strengthens students’ judgment instead of simply making a task faster. Sarah's concern is also real: students may accept suggestions without learning to revise. A student compares an AI suggestion with a writing tutor's comment and keeps only the change that clarifies the claim. The example suggests a way to protect the main benefit while checking for unwanted effects. I would begin with a clear, limited plan and compare access, privacy, and the quality of learning before expanding it. If the evidence shows that some people lose access, the rule should change. This approach is practical because it makes a decision now but leaves room to learn from its results.

title: Recorded Lectures or Live Attendance
targetBand: Mục tiêu luyện tập theo tiêu chí mức 5/5 của rubric Discussion; không bảo đảm điểm Writing 5.5–6.0

prompt.professorQuestion: Today we are looking at recorded lectures or live attendance. Some people argue that universities should record every lecture, while others say that universities should emphasize live attendance. Which argument is more convincing to you? Give a reason and an example.

studentOpinions.stance: To me, universities should record every lecture. Students can revisit difficult explanations after class. This choice addresses a need that people already face, so waiting for a perfect solution may mean doing nothing. Clear guidelines could keep the first step manageable and allow changes later.

I would take a different path: universities should emphasize live attendance. Class questions and discussion are hard to capture on video. The most visible benefit is not always the most important one. If we make a broad change too quickly, some groups may lose an option that currently works for them.

modelEssay: On recorded lectures or live attendance, I would take a middle position, with Michael's idea as the starting point. Students can revisit difficult explanations after class. Still, Sarah is right to worry that class questions and discussion are hard to capture on video. The key is whether the tool strengthens students’ judgment instead of simply making a task faster. A chemistry student replays a five-minute demonstration before attempting the lab but still attends the discussion. A useful test would track access, privacy, and the quality of learning, not just whether the proposal sounds popular. If those measures improve without placing an unfair burden on one group, the change can grow. Otherwise, decision makers should revise it. This is more convincing than treating either student's argument as a rule that works in every situation.

targetBand: Mục tiêu luyện tập theo tiêu chí mức 5/5 của rubric Discussion; không bảo đảm điểm Writing 5.5–6.0

prompt.professorQuestion: For our discussion of automatic translation in class, consider two options: students should use translation tools for difficult readings; alternatively, students should read without automatic translation. What should decision makers prioritize, and why?

title: Student Data in Learning Apps
targetBand: Mục tiêu luyện tập theo tiêu chí mức 5/5 của rubric Discussion; không bảo đảm điểm Writing 5.5–6.0

prompt.professorQuestion: We have been studying student data in learning apps. One view holds that schools should collect app-use data to identify struggling students. A different view is that schools should minimize tracking. Which view do you find more persuasive, and under what conditions?

studentOpinions.stance: My view is that schools should collect app-use data to identify struggling students. Early alerts can direct them to support. This seems like a practical starting point, especially for people who cannot wait for a complete redesign. We can still measure its effects and adjust the program.

I disagree with that priority and think schools should minimize tracking. Private study habits should not become permanent records. Good intentions alone do not guarantee good results. I would first protect the people most likely to face extra costs or lose access.

modelEssay: Michael makes the stronger case on student data in learning apps, provided the change has clear safeguards. Early alerts can direct them to support. Sarah's point deserves attention because private study habits should not become permanent records. I would therefore avoid a one-size-fits-all rule. An adviser receives a warning about missing assignments without seeing a student's browsing history. The key is whether the tool strengthens students’ judgment instead of simply making a task faster. Decision makers could publish results on access, privacy, and the quality of learning after a short trial and invite feedback from the people affected. If the cost is too high or access becomes less fair, they can adjust the policy. That is a more responsible way to act than waiting indefinitely or assuming that a good goal guarantees a good outcome.

prompt.professorQuestion: In our class, we are discussing mindfulness in schools. One proposal is that schools should offer brief mindfulness practice; another is that schools should focus on practical counseling. Which approach would you support, and what limitation would you consider?

studentOpinions.stance: I would support the first approach: schools should offer brief mindfulness practice. Some students can manage stress more easily. The immediate benefit matters because people need a workable solution in everyday life. We could review the results after a short period and improve the details if necessary.

I see a stronger case for the second approach: schools should focus on practical counseling. One exercise will not solve serious problems. A policy can sound promising yet create costs or problems for people it overlooks. Starting with the less disruptive choice would give us time to understand those effects.

prompt.recommendedWords: Ít nhất 100 từ theo đề mẫu ETS; 120–150 từ là mục tiêu luyện tập

modelEssay: I agree more with Michael on mindfulness in schools, although Sarah identifies an important limit. Some students can manage stress more easily. A strategy that helps some people may put pressure on others, so participation should be considered carefully. Sarah's concern is also real: one exercise will not solve serious problems. A school offers an optional five-minute practice and keeps access to trained counselors. The example suggests a way to protect the main benefit while checking for unwanted effects. I would begin with a clear, limited plan and compare participation, stress, and whether habits last before expanding it. If the evidence shows that some people lose access, the rule should change. This approach is practical because it makes a decision now but leaves room to learn from its results.

prompt.professorQuestion: Today we are looking at competition in class. Some people argue that teachers should use friendly competitions, while others say that teachers should avoid ranking students. Which argument is more convincing to you? Give a reason and an example.

I would take a different path: teachers should avoid ranking students. Competition may discourage slower learners. The most visible benefit is not always the most important one. If we make a broad change too quickly, some groups may lose an option that currently works for them.

title: Study Partners
targetBand: Mục tiêu luyện tập theo tiêu chí mức 5/5 của rubric Discussion; không bảo đảm điểm Writing 5.5–6.0

prompt.professorQuestion: For our discussion of study partners, consider two options: courses should assign study partners; alternatively, courses should let students choose partners. What should decision makers prioritize, and why?

studentOpinions.stance: I favor the first view that courses should assign study partners. Students may ask questions more readily with a peer. A small, well-planned change could show whether the idea helps in practice. If it does, decision makers would have a stronger basis for expanding it.

I lean toward the alternative: courses should let students choose partners. Forced pairs can be uncomfortable. We should also ask who pays for the change and who might be left out. Those questions matter before turning one attractive idea into a general rule.

A strategy that helps some people may put pressure on others, so participation should be considered carefully. On the other hand, students may ask questions more readily with a peer. A course offers optional partner matching and a way to switch after two weeks. This is why I would keep the useful part of Michael's proposal in a smaller program and measure participation, stress, and whether habits last. If the results are strong, expansion would be justified. If not, people would still have the existing option. Such a trial respects Sarah's concern while allowing a promising idea to be tested rather than dismissed.

targetBand: Mục tiêu luyện tập theo tiêu chí mức 5/5 của rubric Discussion; không bảo đảm điểm Writing 5.5–6.0

prompt.professorQuestion: We have been studying notifications and focus. One view holds that apps should default to fewer notifications. A different view is that apps should let users decide. Which view do you find more persuasive, and under what conditions?

studentOpinions.stance: My view is that apps should default to fewer notifications. Interruptions can break concentration. This seems like a practical starting point, especially for people who cannot wait for a complete redesign. We can still measure its effects and adjust the program.

I disagree with that priority and think apps should let users decide. Alerts can be important for work and family. Good intentions alone do not guarantee good results. I would first protect the people most likely to face extra costs or lose access.

Sarah's point deserves attention because alerts can be important for work and family. I would therefore avoid a one-size-fits-all rule. A study app starts with quiet mode but lets students enable deadline reminders. A strategy that helps some people may put pressure on others, so participation should be considered carefully. Decision makers could publish results on participation, stress, and whether habits last after a short trial and invite feedback from the people affected. If the cost is too high or access becomes less fair, they can adjust the policy. That is a more responsible way to act than waiting indefinitely or assuming that a good goal guarantees a good outcome.

prompt.professorQuestion: We have been studying public childcare spaces. One view holds that cities should use vacant buildings for childcare centers. A different view is that cities should first support existing providers. Which view do you find more persuasive, and under what conditions?

studentOpinions.stance: My view is that cities should use vacant buildings for childcare centers. Families need convenient care near work. This seems like a practical starting point, especially for people who cannot wait for a complete redesign. We can still measure its effects and adjust the program.

I disagree with that priority and think cities should first support existing providers. New centers require trained staff. Good intentions alone do not guarantee good results. I would first protect the people most likely to face extra costs or lose access.

prompt.recommendedWords: Ít nhất 100 từ theo đề mẫu ETS; 120–150 từ là mục tiêu luyện tập

modelEssay: Michael makes the stronger case on public childcare spaces, provided the change has clear safeguards. Families need convenient care near work. Sarah's point deserves attention because new centers require trained staff. I would therefore avoid a one-size-fits-all rule. A city renovates one suitable building while offering grants to established providers. A service must fit real family schedules and the capacity of the people who provide it. Decision makers could publish results on family schedules, access to support, and staff capacity after a short trial and invite feedback from the people affected. If the cost is too high or access becomes less fair, they can adjust the policy. That is a more responsible way to act than waiting indefinitely or assuming that a good goal guarantees a good outcome.

title: Shared Meals in Communities
targetBand: Mục tiêu luyện tập theo tiêu chí mức 5/5 của rubric Discussion; không bảo đảm điểm Writing 5.5–6.0

prompt.professorQuestion: Our topic this week is shared meals in communities. Imagine a community choosing between these approaches: community centers should host low-cost group meals; centers should focus on food delivery. Which would you recommend? Explain your reasoning with a concrete case.

studentOpinions.stance: I would choose this option: community centers should host low-cost group meals. Neighbors can meet and reduce isolation. It gives people a visible improvement and a way to judge whether the change is working. A limited rollout could keep mistakes from affecting everyone.

I would choose the other option: centers should focus on food delivery. Some residents cannot travel to events. That concern should be addressed before spending money or changing established routines. Otherwise, a policy may solve one problem while creating another.

prompt.recommendedWords: Ít nhất 100 từ theo đề mẫu ETS; 120–150 từ là mục tiêu luyện tập

modelEssay: I partly agree with both students, but I would put Sarah's concern first for shared meals in communities. Some residents cannot travel to events. A service must fit real family schedules and the capacity of the people who provide it. Michael is right that neighbors can meet and reduce isolation. A center offers a weekly meal and delivers portions to housebound neighbors. This case shows that the two goals do not always require an all-or-nothing choice. I would start where the benefit is easiest to measure and keep another option available for people who need it. Comparing family schedules, access to support, and staff capacity would reveal whether the approach works beyond one appealing example. A flexible policy would be easier to defend because it responds to actual results and individual needs.
